events.text: The first disciple of {b3_sect} is still here. The others have come, trained and gone. This one arrived the first winter, with a bundle and no history, and now sweeps the Cloud Tablet hall at dawn, and answers questions with a serene "perhaps." You have not once been able to tell whether this is wisdom or the lack of it.

choices.text: Ask the disciple what they want

effects.log: The disciple considers for a long time and says: "to keep sweeping." You are not sure whether you have been taught or insulted.

choices.text: Send the disciple out to see the world

effects.log: The disciple goes, reluctantly, and returns in a year with exactly the same expression and a very fine pear.

events.text: The first disciple of {b3_sect} has taken to sitting at the gate in the evenings, watching travellers pass. A traveller, a stranger, tells you that the disciple is giving advice, and that it is very good. The traveller is on the second day of a journey they were about to abandon.

choices.text: Ask the disciple to teach a class on advice

effects.log: The disciple refuses with great politeness and instead sits at the head of the class, silently, and the pupils learn in the way water learns a bowl.

choices.text: Let the disciple keep to the gate

effects.log: You let them. The gate becomes the most visited place in the whole of the school, and the disciple is called, in whispers, the Porter.

events.text: The Porter of {b3_sect} is old now, and has stopped speaking altogether. Disciples bring tea and sit beside them. One evening the Porter takes your hand and writes a single word on the palm with a finger. It is your own name, in the hand you used when you were a beginner. Nobody has ever seen that hand.

choices.text: Keep the palm unwashed until the mark fades

effects.log: You keep it. The mark fades in three days, and in those three days you are very gentle with everyone, and the school, noticing, is the same.

choices.text: Write the Porter's name on their palm in return

effects.log: You write it. The Porter smiles, a very small smile, and nods, and does not speak again, and it is the best conversation of your life.

events.text: A young disciple of {b3_sect} has been caught practising a technique that is forbidden: one that belongs to a rival school. The disciple says they learned it from watching a travelling troupe. The elders want the disciple dismissed. The technique is, annoyingly, extremely good.

choices.text: Declare the technique a gift of the troupe and adopt it

effects.log: You adopt it. The elders grumble, and the troupe is thanked and fed, and the sect gains a new form, and a tradition of borrowing well.

choices.text: Forbid it, and reward the disciple for confessing

effects.log: You forbid it. The disciple is rewarded for honesty and keeps the technique in private, and every few years someone sees it, and nods.

events.text: A merchant offers {b3_sect} a great sum to teach his three sons. They are lazy, arrogant and cheerfully stupid. The sect is poor, and the sum would repair the roof of the Cloud Tablet hall. {b3_elder} says an honest teacher does not sell the Way. The roof has a hole in it, directly above your seat.

choices.text: Take the sons and teach them to cook

effects.log: You take them. The sons, to their own bewilderment, become excellent cooks, and the roof is repaired, and the merchant, appalled, is also pleased.

choices.text: Refuse the sum, and bring a bucket

effects.log: You refuse. The bucket sits under the hole for ten years and becomes a feature of the sect, and the merchant sends a gift anyway, unasked.

events.text: The disciples of {b3_sect} have begun, without anyone suggesting it, to leave small gifts at the door of your study: a pebble, a feather, a rice cake. By midwinter the threshold is a pile. A visiting elder of another school remarks that this is how worship starts. You ask whether it is how love starts. The elder has no answer.

choices.text: Accept the gifts and write each disciple a short note

effects.log: You write. The notes are brief and particular, and the disciples keep them for life, and the pile, thereafter, stops growing and starts being used.

choices.text: Leave a gift of your own at each disciple's door

effects.log: You do. The exchange becomes a custom, and the school acquires an unusual and gentle sense of owing each other.

events.text: A disciple of {b3_sect} has stopped sleeping. They sit in the cloud court all night with eyes open, saying they are watching something. In the morning they are cheerful and can describe nothing. A healer examines them and finds them in perfect health. {b3_elder} wants them sent away. They want to stay.

choices.text: Sit the night out with them

effects.log: You sit. At the third hour you see it too: a faint turning of light on the wall, slow, a wheel. You say nothing, and the disciple, beside you, smiles.

choices.text: Send them to rest for a season at a quiet house in the hills

effects.log: You send them. They return rested and speak of the wheel in a different tone, and teach it to six others.

events.text: The kitchen of {b3_sect} has been run for many years by the same cook, who has a fierce temper and a habit of ladling soup with a small flourish. A new disciple, nervous, drops a bowl. The cook rounds on them, then stops, sees their face, and sits them down, and gives them the soup, and says the bowl was always going to break.

choices.text: Speak to the cook, and thank them

effects.log: You thank them. The cook grunts and says it is only soup. The new disciple, three years on, is the sect's best cook.

choices.text: Quietly add a seat for the cook at the elders' table

effects.log: You add it. The cook refuses it for a month, then sits, in stiff silence, and the elders learn a great deal about onions.

events.text: A sudden gift arrives at {b3_sect}: a full set of rare scrolls on breath and stance, from an old friend of a dead master, with a note saying "to be shared with the world." The elders want to keep them within the walls. A young disciple says they should be copied and distributed. The argument takes two days.

choices.text: Copy the scrolls and send them to every school in the region

effects.log: You copy them. The sect's name travels with them, and the school, within a decade, is the most respected in the land.

choices.text: Keep them in the library, but open the doors to any serious reader

effects.log: You open the doors. A trickle of scholars arrives, and the library fills with guests, and arguments, and tea.

events.text: The roof of the Cloud Tablet hall of {b3_sect} leaks on the morning of the school's annual contest. The disciples run for buckets. The visiting masters are seated in a row on cushions under the worst of it. A drop falls on the oldest master's head, and then another. He does not move. He is, they realise, asleep.

choices.text: Hold an umbrella over him until the contest begins

effects.log: You hold it. He wakes in the middle of the first round, says "very good," and goes back to sleep, and is the only one to be dry at the end.

choices.text: Let him sleep, and begin the contest

effects.log: You begin. The master, wet, snores through it, and the drops fall in time to the drums, and the contest is thought the finest ever held.

events.text: A deer has been seen entering the training yard of {b3_sect} at dawn. It stands at the edge, watching the disciples, and leaves when the first drum is struck. One disciple has started leaving rice cakes. Another has started bowing to it. The elders say deer are not teachers. The deer, as if overhearing, turns its head.

choices.text: Bow to the deer yourself

effects.log: You bow. The deer bows its head in return, and the yard goes very quiet, and for a week the stances of the disciples are strangely beautiful.

choices.text: Place a bowl of water at the edge for the deer

effects.log: You place it. The deer drinks every dawn, and then, one morning, brings a fawn, and the sect has its first mascot.

events.text: A dispute between two senior disciples of {b3_sect} has split the school into factions. One holds that the Way is stillness. The other holds that it is motion. They are both right, and each regards the other as a heretic. You are asked to resolve the matter by choosing. The two disciples, in a gesture of maximum hostility, have each made you a cup of tea.

choices.text: Drink both cups, one after the other

effects.log: You drink both. Each is excellent. You say the Way is in the tea, and the factions, wrong-footed, laugh, and the dispute becomes a rivalry about tea.

choices.text: Ask them to spar, one doing only stillness, the other only motion

effects.log: They spar for an hour. It is a draw, and a thing of beauty, and the school understands it has been shown the same thing twice.

events.text: A visiting scholar asks to sit in on the teaching of {b3_sect} and take notes. The scholar is a thorough, humourless person with a large satchel. At the end of the month the scholar presents you with a manuscript describing your teaching method. It is accurate in every detail. It is also, you realise, a method you did not know you had.

choices.text: Read the manuscript aloud to the disciples

effects.log: You read it. The disciples listen in a kind of stunned silence, and then one says, "so that is what we have been doing," and the school is never the same.

choices.text: Put the manuscript on the shelf, and keep teaching as before

effects.log: You shelve it. Years later you take it down and find it is still accurate, and a little more kind than you remember.

events.text: The well in the cloud court of {b3_sect} has gone brackish. The disciples carry water from a spring a mile away. One of them, an apprentice of no distinction, digs at night, secretly, for six weeks. The well comes clear again, sweet and cold. The apprentice is asleep in the dirt beside it, and does not wake for a day.

choices.text: Name the well for the apprentice

effects.log: You name it. The apprentice is mortified, and thrilled, and the name is cut into the stone, and carried by the school as a kind of vow.

choices.text: Let the apprentice sleep, and say nothing until they wake

effects.log: You say nothing. The apprentice wakes, finds the well full, and does not understand why the disciples are all looking at them like that.

events.text: A hush falls on the school of {b3_sect}. No one will say why. In the courtyard a stranger stands holding a small box, and every disciple is at a window. The stranger asks to see the head of the sect. You come out. The stranger opens the box. Inside is a single seed, and the stranger says it is for you, from a person who has long been dead.

choices.text: Plant the seed in the middle of the courtyard

effects.log: You plant it. It sprouts in a week, and in a month it is a sapling, and in a year it bears a fruit nobody can name, which tastes of someone's kitchen.

choices.text: Ask the stranger who sent it

effects.log: The stranger says: "your first teacher." You had not known your first teacher was dead. You thank the stranger and stand in the courtyard, holding the box, a long time.

events.text: A disciple of {b3_sect} comes to you with a quarrel. They have fought with their closest friend, and have not spoken for a month, and cannot remember why. Each waits for the other to speak first. The school is tense. You are asked to settle it. You have not the faintest idea what the quarrel was about.

choices.text: Ask each of them to tell you the quarrel separately, then compare

effects.log: You compare. The two accounts do not overlap at all, and each is sincere, and the pair, hearing, collapse in laughter and make peace.

choices.text: Put them on the same sweeping duty for a week, in silence

effects.log: You do. By the third day they are speaking in whispers, and by the week's end are inseparable again.

events.text: Winter is cruel to {b3_sect} this year, and the stores run low. The disciples start to ration themselves, tightening belts, giving up second helpings. A young disciple, thin as a rake, volunteers to go without altogether. The elders are moved. You notice that the disciple has been secretly feeding the stray dog from his own bowl.

choices.text: Feed the disciple from the head's table and tell him to eat

effects.log: You do. The disciple is embarrassed, and eats, and the dog is fed too, and by spring the dog is the sect's pet, and the disciple a favourite.

choices.text: Quietly send a rider for help to a friendly school

effects.log: You send one. Help arrives in three days with sacks of grain, and the winter is passed without further hardship.

events.text: Two disciples of {b3_sect} are seen on the roof of the Cloud Tablet hall at midnight, in each other's arms. They are caught by the night watch. Both are of age. The rule of the sect says nothing about this. {b3_elder} says the rule says nothing about gravity either, and no one is proposing to repeal it.

choices.text: Say plainly that the rule is silent, and the school should be too

effects.log: You say so. The two are mortified and grateful, and the school keeps its counsel, and the pair are among its most devoted.

choices.text: Add a small rule, that roof-meetings be conducted in daylight, with tea

effects.log: You add it. The school roars. The pair, sheepish, are married by the spring, on the roof, in daylight, with tea.

events.text: A famed sword-master arrives at {b3_sect} to see the school, and spends three days saying nothing. On the fourth he asks to see the youngest disciple, a girl of eleven. He watches her practise, his face a mask. At the end he bows deeply to her and says: "I have been looking for you for sixty years."

choices.text: Ask him what he means

effects.log: He says: "someone who does it for joy." He leaves her his sword, and goes into the mountains, and does not come back.

choices.text: Thank him, and ask whether he will stay as a teacher

effects.log: He stays a season, teaches her nothing, and leaves her his sword when he goes.

events.text: A child is left at the gate of {b3_sect} with a note: "she is gifted, she is dangerous, please." The child, three years old, sits in the dust and draws circles with a stick. Each circle, when completed, hums faintly. The elders pale. They suggest the child be sent away to a school with stronger walls.

choices.text: Take the child in, with a promise to teach her to bear it

effects.log: You take her. She grows up slowly, humming, and the school builds its life around her gentleness, and learns more from her than it teaches.

choices.text: Find a school with stronger walls, and visit often

effects.log: You find one, and visit every season, and the child writes you drawings, and the circles, years later, come to hum your name.

events.text: The annual harvest of {b3_sect}'s terraced garden is the best in memory, and it is gone. A single night, a hundred sacks, nothing left but footprints that lead into the forest and end in a stone circle. The disciples want to burn the forest. The old gardener sits on a step and says it is probably the fox spirit, and that it is hungry.

choices.text: Leave a share of the next harvest at the circle

effects.log: You leave one. The following year the garden is better than ever, and the circle holds a fox pelt, folded, with a note, in awkward characters: "thanks."

choices.text: Set a watch and catch the thief

effects.log: You set a watch. The thief is indeed a fox, thin, and shy, who is fed, and sent home with a bag, and the garden is peaceful.

events.text: The disciples of {b3_sect} hold a festival of lanterns in your honour, without being asked. Hundreds of them hang from every beam, painted with scenes from your life. Some are accurate. Some are, frankly, flattering. One, in the corner, shows you asleep over a book with a smear of ink on your cheek. It is the one you like best.

choices.text: Hang that one in the study

effects.log: You hang it. The disciple who painted it is appointed the school's portraitist, and weeps, and the lantern is lit on every anniversary.

choices.text: Walk among the lanterns, thanking each painter by name

effects.log: You do. It takes until dawn. The disciples are touched beyond speech, and you learn more about them in a night than in a year.

events.text: A traveller, tired and thirsty, is brought into {b3_sect} by two disciples, and fed. In the evening the traveller turns out to be a famous poet in disguise. The poet offers to write a verse in thanks. The disciples are ecstatic. {b3_elder} points out that the poet has a reputation for verses that are secretly rude.

choices.text: Accept the verse and read it aloud at the next feast

effects.log: You read it. It is brilliant, and very slightly rude, and the school adopts it as a motto, and chants it at gatherings, and is secretly pleased.

choices.text: Ask the poet to write the verse in private, and keep it in the library

effects.log: You keep it. The library acquires a hush of its own, and a small, naughty glow.

events.text: The long-promised new training hall of {b3_sect} is at last finished. It smells of cedar. The first morning, the disciples file in, bow, and stand in respectful silence, afraid to scuff the floor. You tell them to begin. No one moves. Only a very small disciple, in the back, steps forward and stamps once, hard.

choices.text: Stamp after the small disciple

effects.log: You stamp. The hall rings, and the disciples laugh, and by the end of the morning the new floor is scuffed in a hundred places and well loved.

choices.text: Praise the small disciple for starting

effects.log: You praise. The small disciple goes scarlet, and the hall, released, begins to move, and by noon it feels like home.

events.text: A pair of sparring disciples of {b3_sect} have injured each other, lightly, in a bout that went further than either meant. Both apologise to the other, at once, and then to you, and then to the hall. They are so contrite that the training master, a stern woman, finds herself hiding a smile.

choices.text: Give them both a week of cooking duty, together

effects.log: You do. They emerge as friends, and a pair of rather good cooks.

choices.text: Use the bout as a lesson for the whole school

effects.log: You do. The training master takes over, and the school learns a good deal about the economy of force.

events.text: The ancient bell of {b3_sect}, which calls the disciples to practice each dawn, goes silent one morning. The ringer pulls the rope and nothing happens. A closer look shows the clapper is gone. The disciples are lost; they have never practised without it. They wait in the yard, unsure, in the grey light.

choices.text: Ring the hour with your own voice

effects.log: You do, a long clear note. The disciples fall into place as if the bell had never failed, and the clapper is found in a rice-jar a week later, with a note: "sorry."

choices.text: Let the disciples begin when they feel ready

effects.log: You let them. They begin, one by one, in silence, and it is the most focused practice of the year.

events.text: A distant noble sends {b3_sect} an invitation to perform at a wedding. The fee is high; the disciples are keen. The elders say the Way is not a show. The noble sends a second note: "my daughter is blind, and has asked to hear a sword." You read it twice.

choices.text: Send a small party to perform a single, quiet form for the bride

effects.log: You send them. The bride listens to the whisper of the blade, and weeps, and the noble sends nothing but gratitude, and the school learns something about its own art.

choices.text: Decline politely, and invite the bride to the school

effects.log: You invite her. She comes, and sits at the edge of the yard for a week, listening, and is changed, and so are the disciples.

events.text: Heavy rains flood the lower the cloud court of {b3_sect}, and the training ground is a lake. The disciples, rolling up their sleeves, drain it for three days. On the fourth morning, in the mud, they find an old stone disc, carved with a pattern of spirals, which hums when struck.

choices.text: Set the disc in the centre of the new yard

effects.log: You set it. Each morning the disc hums when the first foot touches it, and the school, thereafter, begins every day in the same step.

choices.text: Send a rubbing to a scholar of old stone

effects.log: The scholar replies: "a calling-stone for a lost school." The reply is accompanied by a long and rather moving poem.

events.text: A visitor to {b3_sect} announces, with a tremor, that the school's second-in-command is a fraud: that he has never won a bout in his life, that his trophies are bought, and that the visitor has the proof. The second-in-command, listening at the door, comes in and says: it is all true. He has always taught well, he says, and has never claimed otherwise.

choices.text: Ask the disciples what they have learned from him

effects.log: They answer, one after another. The list is long and moving, and the visitor, who came for blood, goes quiet, and the school is, if anything, closer.

choices.text: Ask the visitor to teach for a week in his place

effects.log: The visitor tries. He is a brilliant fighter and an atrocious teacher, and the second-in-command, restored, is greeted by a standing ovation.

events.text: The graduating disciples of {b3_sect} stand in a row before you, each to receive a final word. You have the same word for each, prepared: a short saying, copied from your own teacher. It has served you for years. Looking at the last in the row, a stubborn, tearful girl, you realise the saying is not enough for her.

choices.text: Say something different, and honest

effects.log: You say it. The girl blinks, nods, and goes, and the school hears the words, and twenty years later they are carved over the gate.

choices.text: Give her the saying anyway, and add your hand on her shoulder

effects.log: You do. She goes, strangely comforted, and the saying, thereafter, means something new to you too.

events.text: A rumour goes round that {b3_sect} teaches a secret technique that makes the user invisible. Applicants swarm the gate. You explain, at length, that there is no such technique. They do not believe you. A disciple, helpful, demonstrates "invisibility" by standing still in a corner for an hour. Eleven applicants are impressed.

choices.text: Admit the eleven as a class on standing still

effects.log: You admit them. They are, at the end of a year, the calmest people in the district, and the rumour, thereafter, is quietly true.

choices.text: Send them all away with a bowl of soup

effects.log: You send them off with soup. The rumour doubles in the telling, and your gate, thereafter, has a queue of the hopeful that you feed every winter.

events.text: The students of {b3_sect} stage a mock trial of their own teacher, in which you are accused of making the lessons too hard. The prosecutor, a girl of fifteen, is relentless. The defence, a boy with a cold, is hopeless. The jury, a row of cooks, is sullen. The judge is a goat.

choices.text: Testify in your own defence, and lose

effects.log: You testify and lose, to cheers. The sentence is a week of easy lessons, which you carry out so badly that the students beg you to resume.

choices.text: Bribe the goat

effects.log: You bribe it with a carrot. The goat acquits, and the prosecutor, scarlet, protests that the court has been corrupted, which is the best lesson of the term.

events.text: A widow arrives at {b3_sect} with a sack of coins, her late husband's savings, and a request that the school take her son. The boy is hollow-eyed and silent. The widow says he has not spoken since the funeral. The elders are reluctant. You are not sure the school is the right place for a child in grief.

choices.text: Take the boy as a houseboy, not a pupil, and let him follow you about

effects.log: You do. He follows, silent, for a year. In the second year he speaks, once, to ask the name of a bird, and the school nearly weeps.

choices.text: Send the sack back and recommend a gentler house in the hills

effects.log: You do. The widow thanks you with tears, and the boy writes, three years later, a short letter that begins "I am better."

events.text: A lantern festival is held in the town below {b3_sect}, and the disciples, forbidden to go, peer through the gate at the glow. A small, stubborn disciple has slipped out. The master of discipline is livid. The disciple is found at dawn, asleep on the town bridge, holding a paper lantern, smiling.

choices.text: Forgive the disciple, and light the lantern in the school's courtyard

effects.log: You do. The lantern glows all night, and the disciple is sent to bed, and the school is quietly allowed to go to the next festival.

choices.text: Apply the school's penalty, kindly, and keep the lantern on the shelf

effects.log: You apply it. The disciple serves it cheerfully, and the lantern on the shelf is the last thing most visitors remark upon.

events.text: Your old teacher visits {b3_sect}, grey and slow, leaning on a stick. The disciples are in awe. The old teacher walks the halls, nodding. At the door of your study they stop, and look at the chair behind the desk. "Smaller than I thought," they say, and then, "it suits you." It is the nearest you have come to praise from them in thirty years.

choices.text: Offer the chair to your old teacher

effects.log: The old teacher sits, and sighs, and says it is a good chair, and will not get up for an hour, and you stand, and learn what it is to be a student again.

choices.text: Pour tea, and sit on the floor

effects.log: You sit on the floor. The old teacher laughs, a rusty sound, and sits beside you, and the two of you share a silence you remember from forty years ago.

events.text: The elders of the sect that has come under {b3_sect} are very correct. They bow, offer tea, present the school's register, and leave a space at the end of the row where your seal will go. Their eyes are polite and dead. You understand that you are being given everything except what you wanted.

choices.text: Ask them to stay on as your councillors, not your subjects

effects.log: You ask. They are shocked, and then slowly interested, and over a year the dead eyes warm, and the school becomes a wing of yours rather than a prize.

choices.text: Keep the register, return the seal, and ask nothing else

effects.log: You keep the register and return the seal. They bow, puzzled, and send you a tea-set at the new year, with a note that is almost friendly.

events.text: A young disciple of the school you have brought under {b3_sect} arrives at your gate with a bundle and a hostile look. They have been sent to learn what you did, and to hate it. They are given a bed in the dormitory and a bowl of congee. Within a week the disciple has been absorbed into a card game, and forgotten to hate.

choices.text: Invite the disciple to your table and ask what they want to learn

effects.log: You invite. The disciple, flustered, says: "everything," and you spend the winter on everything, and the two schools are joined at the roots.

choices.text: Leave the disciple to the card game and its consequences

effects.log: You leave them. They learn the school's habits from the bottom, and return home with a dozen friends, and a persistent cough.

events.text: The old master of the school that came to heel stands in your the cloud court, stiff, in the robes of his school, holding a sword he has not drawn in a decade. He has come to be released from his oath. He says he cannot be second to anyone. He asks for a duel. He is eighty and trembles. The whole school watches.

choices.text: Accept the duel, and fight with a wooden staff

effects.log: You fight with a staff, and lose, on purpose, in a way that cannot be seen. He bows, satisfied, and his school, watching, understands, and is silent.

choices.text: Decline, and offer him the right to teach in your hall as a guest of honour

effects.log: You offer. He stands a long moment, then sheathes the sword, and says "I have not been asked to teach in a long time." His voice is not steady.

events.text: The two schools now under your name hold a joint assembly for the first time. The seats are arranged in two rows. Nobody sits. They stand, glaring across the aisle, each waiting for the other to take a seat. You walk in and sit on the floor in the middle of the aisle. After a minute, someone sits beside you. Then another.

choices.text: Stay on the floor until both schools are seated around you

effects.log: You stay. It takes an hour. The assembly, when it begins, is a circle, and no one says who arranged it.

choices.text: Rise, and call for the tea

effects.log: You rise and call. The tea arrives, in mismatched cups from both kitchens, and the assembly proceeds with a clatter of crockery that is the sound of a new school.

events.text: A treasure of the school that came to heel has gone missing: a plain wooden mask, said to contain the school's first master. The school accuses yours. Your school accuses theirs. You find the mask in the lap of a sleeping child of the joint kitchen, who had been using it to scare the cats.

choices.text: Return the mask with a solemn apology from both sides

effects.log: You return it. Both schools apologise at once, in a tangle, and the child is given a gift of sweets, and the mask a new, firmer shelf.

choices.text: Let the child keep the mask for a week, supervised

effects.log: You let her. By week's end the cats have gone, the mask is polished, and the child has become the school's unofficial keeper of its history.

events.text: The first harvest of the combined lands of {b3_sect} and the school under it is large. Too large. Both sides claim the surplus. A formal petition arrives from each, in the elaborate prose of the dispute-prone. The two are the same length, to the word. It is clear they were written together, over wine.

choices.text: Divide the surplus by weight, and throw the petitions into the stove

effects.log: You do. The stove warms the room all evening, and the two schools drink the rest of the wine together and call it a festival.

choices.text: Put the surplus toward a shared hall, to be named by lot

effects.log: You do. The hall is built and named the Hall of the Equal Petitions, and is laughed at, and used constantly.

events.text: The disciples of the two schools have been exchanging gifts: small, pointed ones, intended as insults. A box of bad tea. A dull knife. A book of etiquette with the pages glued. By the third month the gifts are more thoughtful. By the sixth, one disciple sends another a warm scarf with a note: "your last gift was excellent. This is my reply."

choices.text: Quietly add to the exchange with a gift of your own for each school

effects.log: You do. The exchange swells into a festival of mock-insult, and the schools are bound by it as by no treaty.

choices.text: Leave the exchange alone, and watch it grow

effects.log: You leave it. It grows into a tradition, and in a hundred years no one will recall it began as a feud.

events.text: The head of the sect you have subdued has been seen walking alone on the ridge each evening. Your people say it is brooding. You climb up one evening to join them. The head does not turn. "I was not good at this," they say. "I knew it for thirty years. You did not make me worse at it; you only said it aloud."

choices.text: Sit down beside them and say nothing

effects.log: You sit. The sun goes down. When you rise, the head says, "thank you for the silence," and the matter between you is never raised again.

choices.text: Say that they led better than they knew

effects.log: You say so. The head laughs, a bitter short laugh, and then a longer one. It is the first sign in years that they are not alone.

events.text: The vanquished school's great library is moved to your halls on forty carts. The scribes go through it for a month and find something none expected: a scroll, in the neat hand of the vanquished school's own founder, praising yours. It was written a century before either school existed, and addressed, in advance, to its rival.

choices.text: Display the scroll in both libraries

effects.log: You do. The two schools stand before it in stunned silence, and the founders' kinship is understood, and the old feud, in its roots, is a family quarrel.

choices.text: Send it to a scholar of old hands to confirm its age

effects.log: The scholar confirms it, and is nearly in tears. The news travels, and the two schools receive more visitors in a year than in a decade.

events.text: A child of the school brought to heel has been placed in a classroom of yours, among the youngest. The child is bright and sulky. On the first day, a disciple of yours takes the child aside and says: "you do not have to love us. You only have to eat lunch." The child, for the first time, smiles.

choices.text: Take that disciple aside and tell them they have done well

effects.log: You do. The disciple, shy, is moved, and becomes a teacher of the very young within the year.

choices.text: Leave the child with lunch, and keep your distance

effects.log: You leave. The child, in time, is the first to cross the border of the two schools with a basket of food, and starts a custom.

events.text: {npc} comes home from the road with a scar across one hand, a bag of letters, and a small, stubborn jar of something that smells of old trees. {He} sets the jar on your desk and says it was given by a person who would not give a name. {He} says it must be opened under a particular moon. {He} cannot remember which.

choices.text: Open it under tonight's moon and see

effects.log: You open it. The jar holds a seed, and a note: "plant at the gate." {npc} is mortified, and you plant it, and in a year there is a tree at the gate with silver leaves.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to tell the whole story of the jar

effects.log: {npc} tells it for three hours. It involves a ferry, a quarrel with a goose, and a stranger on a cliff. By the end, you both suspect the jar is a joke, and are both pleased.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road with an unexpected companion: a young person from a faraway school, who has followed {him} home in the hope of becoming a disciple. {He} did not invite them. {He} says they were persistent, and also that they carried the bags the whole way. The newcomer stands at the gate, politely, hopeful.

choices.text: Admit the newcomer as a guest for a season

effects.log: You admit them. They turn out to be gifted and over-grateful, and {npc} takes them under {his} wing, and you are, in a year, a larger school.

choices.text: Send the newcomer home with a letter and a blessing

effects.log: You send them. {npc} is crestfallen, then relieved. The newcomer returns five years later, tempered, and is admitted by acclamation.

events.text: Among the letters {npc} brings home from the road is one addressed to you in a clumsy hand, from a village in the hills. It is a letter of thanks. A year ago, {npc} had stopped there for a night, and had, without being asked, mended a roof. The village wishes to send you a cow. {npc} insists it was nothing. The cow is at the gate.

choices.text: Accept the cow, and name it after the village

effects.log: You accept. The cow is a placid, enormous animal, and the school is delighted, and {npc} is mocked about the roof for a decade.

choices.text: Send the cow back with a gift of seed, and a letter

effects.log: You send the cow back. The village, touched, sends the cow again at the new year, and the cow, plainly, prefers your school.

events.text: {npc} has returned from the road changed. {He} is quieter. {He} walks more slowly. At the evening meal {he} does not speak, and when asked, says that on the road {he} saw a thing that {he} cannot explain: a village that had lost its name. The people did not mind. They had given up counting years.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to describe the village in full

effects.log: {npc} describes it, haltingly, over three evenings. It is a very particular place, and by the end you want to visit, and are afraid to.

choices.text: Let {npc} rest, and give {him} the quiet room

effects.log: You give {him} the room. {npc} sleeps for two days, and wakes calm, and is soon teaching again, with a gentler hand.

events.text: {npc} comes home with a challenge, addressed to you, from a rival school across the mountains. It is written in beautiful characters, on thick cream paper, and it is, {he} admits, rather rude. {He} tried to refuse it on your behalf. The messenger would not leave. The messenger is still at the gate, drinking tea.

choices.text: Accept the challenge, and set the day

effects.log: You accept. The day comes, and you meet the rival head on a bridge, and the duel is more of a conversation than a fight, and ends in a draw and a friendship.

choices.text: Answer with a gift of tea and a long, courteous letter

effects.log: You answer so. The rival, caught off guard, replies with equal warmth, and the correspondence, over the years, is a model of enemies being kind.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road with twelve cats. They were, {he} says, in the way. They have followed {him} from a far town, along the roads and across a river, and now sit in a row in the courtyard, watching the school with the blank dignity of those who have arrived. A cook, past all patience, begins to count them.

choices.text: Take the cats in, all twelve

effects.log: You take them. The school acquires a quiet, shifting, whiskered presence, and the library is guarded ever after against mice and tedium.

choices.text: Find homes for the cats among the neighbouring villages

effects.log: You find them. {npc} goes door to door with a cat under each arm, and returns with a story for each, and the school hears them all.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road weeping. {He} cannot say why at first. After an hour, {he} tells you: at a crossroads, {he} met a boy, hungry, and gave the boy {his} last rice-cake, and walked on. The boy was at the next crossroads, and the next. {He} realises the boy was never real, and that it was {he} who was being tested, and failed.

choices.text: Tell {npc} that giving the last rice-cake was the test, and {he} passed

effects.log: You tell {him}. {npc} stares, then understands, and the grief breaks into something close to laughter, and {he} returns to the road, a year later, with a sack of rice.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} and let {him} weep

effects.log: You sit. When {he} is done, {he} washes {his} face and goes to practice, and says nothing of it, but is gentler with every hungry creature from that day.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road carrying a very large and ugly rock. {He} says it was a gift, from a hermit. {He} explains that the hermit said the rock "will tell you when it is time." {He} does not know what that means. The rock is set on the shelf in your study. For a week, it sits there, being a rock.

choices.text: Study the rock in the evenings, with patience

effects.log: You study. On the ninth night it is faintly warm, and on the tenth, you hear it hum, and by the end of the month you know what it was telling you, and you act.

choices.text: Put the rock in the garden

effects.log: You put it out. It becomes a favourite seat, and the disciples, with no explanation, sit on it when they need to decide something, and decide well.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road and presents you with a bill. It runs to nineteen pages and itemises: two broken carts, one borrowed donkey, a meal for a family of seven, and the replacement of a bridge plank. At the bottom is a note: "Everything on the list was necessary. Some was also fun." The total is a modest sum.

choices.text: Pay it in full and ask {npc} for a short account of the fun

effects.log: You pay and ask. {npc} writes three pages, shyly, and the account of the bridge plank is the best prose the school has produced in years.

choices.text: Frame the bill and hang it in the dormitory

effects.log: You frame it. The dormitory acquires, along with the bill, an unspoken permission to be a little bit useful in the world.

events.text: {npc} returns, as {he} said {he} would, in exactly two years. {He} is wearing a hat nobody has seen before. It is an impossible hat, tall and orange, with a tassel. {He} says it was a gift, and that it would be rude to take it off. The school stares. {npc} stares back, with enormous dignity.

choices.text: Ask to try the hat on

effects.log: You try it on. It fits perfectly, and the school, in the face of such absurd nobility, falls about laughing, and {npc} beams.

choices.text: Compliment the hat, solemnly

effects.log: You compliment it. {npc} bows, deeply, and wears the hat to every ceremony for the rest of {his} life.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road to find that someone else has taken {his} bed. The newcomer is a disciple admitted while {he} was gone, a quiet young man who has been very careful not to touch anything. {npc} stands in the dormitory door with a bag, uncertain. The newcomer, hearing, leaps up, apologises, and begins to pack.

choices.text: Tell the newcomer to stay, and find {npc} another bed

effects.log: You do. The two become friends, and between them the dormitory acquires a shelf of books.

choices.text: Put them in the same room for a month, and see

effects.log: You do. By the end of the month they have stopped saying sorry, and started saying "your turn," and it is as good as a friendship ever gets.

events.text: {npc} returns from the road with the news that the school's name is known in places you have never heard of. A stranger, three provinces away, sang a song about the founder, and had the tune wrong. {npc} corrected the tune, shyly, and was embraced. {He} has the new verse, and sings it, off-key, in the courtyard. The school listens, wide-eyed.

choices.text: Learn the song and sing it at the next feast

effects.log: You learn it. The feast is a roar of off-key joy, and the school understands for the first time that it has a place in other people's lives.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to write down every verse as heard

effects.log: {npc} writes seven, and the collection is bound and shelved, and is, a century later, the only record of the school's early fame.
